learningObjectives.title: Communicating a message to an audience

questions.q: In typography, what is a 'serif'?
options: A small stroke or line attached to the end of a letterform
The space between two lines of text
A typeface with no decorative strokes
The overall weight of a font
questions.explain: Serifs are the small finishing strokes on letters, seen in typefaces such as Times New Roman.

questions.q: What does the term 'sans-serif' mean?
options: A typeface used only for headings
questions.explain: 'Sans' means 'without', so sans-serif typefaces such as Helvetica have no serif strokes.

questions.q: What does 'kerning' refer to in typography?
options: Adjusting the space between individual pairs of letters
The vertical space between lines of text
The thickness of a letter's stroke
Aligning text to a central axis
questions.explain: Kerning fine-tunes the spacing between specific letter pairs to improve visual balance.

questions.q: Which term describes the vertical spacing between lines of text?
questions.explain: Leading is the spacing between baselines of consecutive lines of type, affecting readability.

questions.q: What does the colour model 'CMYK' stand for?
questions.explain: CMYK is the subtractive colour model used for printing, where K stands for the key (black) plate.

questions.q: The RGB colour model is primarily used for which type of output?
questions.explain: RGB (Red, Green, Blue) is an additive model used for screens such as monitors and phones.

questions.q: On the colour wheel, complementary colours are those that are:
options: The same hue at different tones
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel and create strong visual contrast when paired.

questions.q: In traditional colour theory, which set lists the three primary colours?
questions.explain: In traditional (subtractive) colour theory the primaries are red, yellow and blue, from which other colours are mixed.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of establishing a 'visual hierarchy' in a layout?
options: To guide the viewer's eye to the most important information first
To fill all available space with content
To make every element the same size
To reduce the number of colours used
questions.explain: Visual hierarchy uses size, weight, colour and position to order information by importance.

questions.q: Why is 'white space' (negative space) valuable in a layout?
options: It reduces clutter and improves clarity and focus
It always means the design is unfinished
It saves on printing ink costs
It hides mistakes in the design
questions.explain: White space gives elements room to breathe, improving legibility and directing attention.

questions.q: What is the main function of a grid system in graphic design?
options: To organise and align elements consistently across a layout
To add decorative texture to the background
To convert images from colour to greyscale
To measure the file size of a document
questions.explain: Grids provide structure, helping designers align text and images for a coherent, balanced composition.

questions.q: A key advantage of a vector image over a raster image is that it can be:
options: Scaled to any size without loss of quality
Printed only in black and white
questions.explain: Vectors use mathematical paths, so they remain sharp at any size, unlike pixel-based raster images.

questions.q: A raster (bitmap) image is made up of:
questions.explain: Raster images such as photographs are composed of pixels and lose quality when enlarged.

questions.q: Which Adobe software is primarily designed for creating vector graphics?
questions.explain: Illustrator is a vector-based program, whereas Photoshop is chiefly used for raster image editing.

questions.q: A designer needs to create a logo that will be printed on both a business card and a large banner. Which approach is most suitable?
options: Create it as a vector graphic
Create it as a low-resolution raster JPEG
Photograph a hand-drawn version at small size
Design it only in RGB at 72 dpi
questions.explain: A vector logo scales cleanly from tiny to huge without losing quality, unlike a fixed-pixel raster file.

questions.q: A student is preparing a poster to be professionally printed. Which colour mode should they set the document to?
questions.explain: Professional print uses the CMYK model, so setting it early ensures printed colours match expectations.

questions.q: What is the central aim of graphic communication?
options: To convey a message or information visually to an audience
To document scientific experiments in writing
questions.explain: Graphic communication combines image and text to communicate ideas clearly to a target audience.

questions.q: A designer is creating packaging for a range of children's toys. Which choice best suits this audience?
options: Bright, playful colours and bold, rounded type
Muted greys with small, formal serif text
Dense blocks of technical small print
A monochrome minimalist layout with no imagery
questions.explain: Design decisions must match the audience; children respond to bright, friendly and playful visual language.

questions.q: In graphic communication, what is meant by the 'target audience'?
options: The specific group of people a design is intended to reach
The printer used to produce the work
The software used to create the design
The colour palette chosen for a project
questions.explain: Identifying the target audience shapes the tone, imagery and style so the message connects effectively.

questions.q: A company wants a symbol that is instantly recognisable and reinforces its brand identity. What are they most likely commissioning?
questions.explain: A logo is a distinctive graphic mark designed to be memorable and to represent a brand's identity.
